props.title: Going Berserk

sections.content: Going Berserk represents a fascinating intersection of early 1980s comedy talent, particularly as a vehicle for John Candy during his SCTV period but before his breakout in Splash (1984). The film follows a similar anarchic comedy style to Airplane! (1980) and The Kentucky Fried Movie (1977), though with less consistent results. Director David Steinberg, himself a comedy veteran, attempted to capture the rising tide of sketch-comedy-to-film transitions that defined early 80s humor, similar to what would later succeed with This Is Spinal Tap (1984).

sections.content: The early 1980s marked a crucial period for comedy film evolution, particularly in how sketch comedy performers transitioned to feature films. While Going Berserk didn't achieve the success of later John Candy vehicles like Uncle Buck (1989) or Planes, Trains and Automobiles (1987), it captures a specific moment when the SCTV style of comedy was trying to find its big-screen voice. The film's mix of cult brainwashing plots and oddball character moments feels like a testing ground for what would later work in films like Stripes (1981) and Ghostbusters (1984).

The supporting cast includes Eugene Levy and Joe Flaherty, making this essentially an SCTV reunion film. This positions Going Berserk as part of the Canadian comedy invasion that included Strange Brew (1983) and would later influence films like Brain Candy (1996) from The Kids in the Hall. The movie's scattered plot about a limo driver getting caught up in conspiracy theories and cult activities feels like a precursor to later fish-out-of-water comedies that would become Candy's specialty. sections.content: While Going Berserk may be considered a minor entry in the John Candy filmography, it represents an important bridge between television sketch comedy and feature films. The movie's structure, which often feels like loosely connected comedy scenes, reflects how sketch performers were learning to sustain characters and stories for feature length. This transition period would eventually lead to more polished films like Three Men and a Baby (1987) and Ghostbusters (1984), where sketch comedy performers found their footing in more conventional narratives.
